BILL NUMBER:  S4306

 TITLE OF BILL :
An act to amend the penal law, in relation to property interests


 PURPOSE :
This bill amends Chapter 601 of the laws of 2008, pursuant to an
agreement reached between the legislature and the Governor. This
amendment clarifies that damaging property in which another person has
an ownership interest can constitute criminal mischief, even if the
person who destroys the property or any other person also has an
interest in that property. This amendment eliminates the newly added
requirement of explicit consent from co-owners as a pre-requisite to a
person's reasonable belief that he or she has a right to damage
property in which he or she shares an ownership interest with another.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :
Penal Law section 145.13 defining "property of another" for the
purposes of the crime of criminal mischief and other related offenses
is amended to provide that property of another includes all property
in which another person has an ownership interest, regardless of
whether or not a person who damages such property, or any other
person, also has an interest in such property.  The bill removes a
requirement of explicit consent from co-owners as a pre-requisite to a
person's reasonable belief that he or she has a right to damage
property in which he or she shares an ownership interest with another.

 JUSTIFICATION :
Article 145 of the Penal Law pertaining to criminal mischief and
related offenses did not define "property of another" prior to
November 1, 2008. Effective November 1, 2008, Chapter 601 of the laws
of 2008 amended the Penal Law by adding a new section 145.13 providing
a definition. Chapter 601 responded to cases in which this lack of a
definition enabled one joint owner (such as a spouse) to intimidate or
terrorize the other joint owner by damaging or destroying property
owned by the two parties without fear of criminal consequences. This
issue occurred with increasing frequency throughout the State and the
courts struggled with the interpretation of the criminal mischief
statute as it applied to these situations.  There was particular
concern with and criticism of the interpretation of "property of
another" for the purposes of the crime of criminal mischief by the
appellate court in its decision in People v.  Person, 239 A.D.2d
612,658 N.Y.S.2d 372 (2nd Dept. 1997), in which, in the absence of a
statutory definition, the Court interpreted this language to exclude
property in which an actor has an ownership interest, even if others
have such interests as well.

To avoid confusion and address the need for clarity in the law, the
legislature added a new section, 145.13 to Article 145 of the Penal
Law, providing for a definition of "property of another" pertaining to
criminal mischief and related offenses. It also added a provision
making explicit consent by a co-owner a prerequisite to another
co-owner's ability to damage jointly or co-owned property without the
potential of criminal consequences.

The Governor signed the bill proposed by the legislature in 2008
adding the definitional section 145.13 to Article 145 of the Penal
Law, upon agreement of the legislature to a chapter amendment removing
any rigid requirement in section 145.13 of explicit consent from
co-owners.

In his Approval Memorandum, the Governor acknowledged the importance
of defining property of another pertaining to criminal mischief and
related offenses and noted that a spousal relationship or other basis
of joint ownership should not protect a bad actor from criminal
sanction. However, in his Approval Memorandum, the Governor raised
concerns about a requirement of explicit consent from co-owners as a
prerequisite to another co-owner's ability to damage jointly or
co-owned property without the potential of criminal consequences,
noting that under certain circumstances a spouse or other co-owner may
damage or discard jointly owned property based on consent that is
implied rather than expressed.

This bill refines the newly added definition of "property of another"
under section 145.13 of the Penal Law. It retains protections for a
person who acts based on a reasonable belief by removing the
additional requirement of explicit consent from co-owners as a
pre-requisite to an actor's reasonable belief that he or she has a
right to damage property in which he or she shares an ownership
interest with another.

This bill protects victims of domestic violence, particularly in cases
where there is a shared ownership interest in property, and also
preserves protections previously in place for persons acting under a
reasonable belief.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :
2008: A.6308-A/S.2061-A - Ch.601 '08
2007:  A.6308/S.2061-A.Codes/S.Codes
2006: A.10448/S.6518 - A.Codes/S.Codes

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
None.

 LOCAL FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :
None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
Immediately.

summary: Expands definition of "property of another", for purposes of criminal mischief, to include any property another person has an interest in, regardless of whether the defendant has an interest in such property.
